Thence
THENS
adverb
Saxon thanon, from that place; the demonstrative answering to the interrogative whence. It renders the Hebrew mi-sham, “from there,” and the Greek ekeithen.

Biblical Definition

Thence marks a departure point that God has fixed, and the word carries more theological weight than its four letters suggest. It is the word of the river that waters Eden and “from thence it was parted, and became into four heads” (Gen 2:10) — one source, four streams, the pattern of a blessing that divides without diminishing. It is the word of Babel, where the LORD scattered the builders abroad from thence, so that the place of man’s proudest gathering became the point of his dispersion. It is the word of gospel promise in the mouth of Moses: “if from thence thou shalt seek the LORD thy God, thou shalt find him, if thou seek him with all thy heart” (Deu 4:29) — and the thence there is exile, the far country, the very place of judgment. This is the astonishing thing: God names the place of chastisement as a place from which He may still be sought and found. And it is the word of solemn warning in our Lord’s mouth, “Thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing” (Mat 5:26) — a prison whose thence has no exit, because the debt can never be discharged by the debtor. Two thences, then: one a place God bids you seek Him from, the other a place from which none returns.

Webster 1828 Definition

From that place; from that time; for that reason. The demonstrative of origin, answering to the interrogative whence.

expand to see more

THENCE, adv. From that place: he departed thence.

From that time; thenceforward.

For that reason; from that ground or premise.

Saxon thanon, from that; correlative to whence.

The redundant form from thence is idiomatic in the Authorized Version (Gen 2:10).

Key Scripture

Gen 2:10 — "And a river went out of Eden to water the garden; and from thence it was parted, and became into four heads."

Gen 11:9 — "Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth: and from thence did the LORD scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth."

Deu 4:29 — "But if from thence thou shalt seek the LORD thy God, thou shalt find him, if thou seek him with all thy heart and with all thy soul."

Mat 5:26 — "Verily I say unto thee, Thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing."

Modern Corruption

Deu 4:29 is regularly lifted out of its exile setting and preached as a promise that sincere seeking of any kind finds God — which reverses the covenant order and flatters the seeker.

expand to see more

The corruption is decontextualising. Deu 4:29 is quoted on posters and in devotionals as a general assurance that anyone who looks hard enough will find God, and the thence is quietly dropped. But the thence is the whole point: Moses is describing Israel scattered among the nations under covenant judgment for idolatry, and he promises that even from that place, if they seek with all the heart and all the soul, God will be found. It is a promise to a chastened covenant people, not a general law of religious effort. Strip the setting and it becomes a doctrine of works — seek sincerely, and God is obliged. Scripture never says that. It says no man seeks after God at all until God first seeks him, and the seeking that finds is itself the fruit of grace already at work.

Recover the plain sense: the promise is better than the counterfeit, not weaker. It says that no distance of exile puts a covenant child beyond recovery, that the place of discipline is not the place of abandonment, and that the God who scattered from Babel is the God who says seek me from thence. Set it beside Mat 5:26 and the mercy sharpens. There is a thence from which men are called back and a thence from which they never come out. The difference is not the earnestness of the prisoner but whether the debt has been paid by Another.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Saxon thanon, from that place — the fixed point of departure, whether of blessing, of scattering, or of return.

expand to see more

Thence — Saxon thanon, from that place; correlative of whence.

Hebrew mi-sham, from there (Gen 2:10; Deu 4:29).

Greek ekeithen, from that place (Mat 5:26).

From thence is the AV's settled idiom, redundant but emphatic.

Gen 11:9 makes Babel a thence of scattering; Deu 4:29 makes exile a thence of seeking.

Usage

"Gen 2:10: one river parted from thence — a source that divides without loss."

"Deu 4:29 must be preached with its thence: it is a promise to the chastened, not a formula for the sincere."

"Mat 5:26 names a place with no thence — no exit until an unpayable debt is paid."
